A rise in R*, together with an expected increase in the term premium resulting from the Fed’s balance-sheet normalization, may signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset-market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, stronger growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back monetary easing. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies recorded broad-based cyclical expansions (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real GDP recording positive growth for an eighth consecutive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continued to signal that they would maintain accommodative monetary policies amid subdued inflation, the brighter growth outlooks in Europe and Japan—and the continued tightening of Japan’s labour market—have led some market participants to project further scaling back of quantitative easing programmes in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP of selected Euro area member states Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, recent examples being the announcement in January 2018 of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines and the announcement in early March of import tariffs on steel and aluminium, raising concerns over whether its trading partners might respond with retaliatory measures. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom and other European Union countries are currently negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process subject to considerable uncertainty. If these developments lead to increased trade tensions, they could impede global trade and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions—such as a military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East, or latent terrorist attack risks—could increase global financial market volatility. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year with a robust performance. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the principal driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided steady support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted regional exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressure has remained subdued thus far. In the second half of 2017, overall inflation in East Asia moderated amid lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation excluding food and energy remained low, owing to sluggish wage growth in several economies. Chart 2.9 East Asia: Overall and core consumer price inflation* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and central banks. The improving economy, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, led to significant increases in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Capital inflows into regional markets rallied significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various regional financial assets also rose with the markets. Indeed, credit risk premiums in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained robust growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Hong Kong’s economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although local inflationary pressure should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% sequentially in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow robustly and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was robust on the back of favourable employment and income conditions, continued optimism in consumer sentiment, and the positive wealth effect arising from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activity weakened, increased corporate capital spending caused aggregate investment spending to rise markedly in the final quarter after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net trade in goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment increased by approximately 0.7% to more than 3.85 million, with the most notable increases recorded in construction; financing and business services; and public administration, social and personal services. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance will continue to benefit from an improved global growth outlook and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly because of favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. Regarding domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activity should grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. Although the improved economic environment will stimulate business capital spending, possible interest rate increases may have an adverse impact. The Government projects real GDP growth of 3% to 4% in 2018, while growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in the preceding chapters, the performance of the Mainland Chinese economy amid tightening financial conditions, and developments in Hong Kong’s asset markets. Local inflationary pressure remained contained in the second half of 2017, although sequential inflation momentum showed signs of edging up in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of approximately 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The recovery in fresh-letting private residential rental since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressure remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita payroll Since global inflation remains moderate and domestic cost increases are stable, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressure is expected to remain moderate in 2018, although underlying inflation may gradually rise from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, inflationary pressure may increase in the second half of 2018 owing to the pass-through effect of growth in fresh-letting private residential rental. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2018 is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government projects an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, any stronger-than-expected increase in global inflation or commodity prices could add to local inflation momentum. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and any substantial tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the low interest rate environment after the 2008 global financial crisis, Hong Kong households’ mortgage debt increased. As the normalisation of US interest rates proceeds, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise in tandem with US interest rates, correspondingly increasing households’ mortgage repayment burden in the future and thereby weighing on household consumption. This box therefore examines the impact of an increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to mortgage debt-service payments—that is, interest payments plus loan principal repayments—as a proportion of income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of an interest rate shock to private consumption. In addition to the substitution and income effects generally discussed in economic theory, as well as the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices, where there is a mortgage repayment burden, an interest rate shock will also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and, in turn, households’ disposable income. This impact will increase as the amount of outstanding mortgage loans rises. In addition, principal repayments will vary with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, which will also affect private consumption by changing households’ disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the outstanding mortgage debt-servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the existing mortgage repayment burden indicator, which applies only to new mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the household sector, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector; Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households, proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of such households; and rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt-servicing burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, together with the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. Both ratios trended downwards in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in aggregate household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the housing market bubble in 1997 and the sharp fall in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite the sharp increase in property prices following the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable because the HKMA’s macro-prudential measures on banks’ mortgage lending restrained aggregate household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of maturities for new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income We also compare the OMDSR with banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which is the actual debt-servicing-to-income ratio of banks’ new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks’ debt-servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As housing prices were lower when existing mortgages were originated, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages—that is, the OMDSR—is lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages—that is, banks’ debt-servicing ratio. Moreover, banks’ debt-servicing ratio is higher because, in compliance with the HKMA’s prudential regulatory requirements, banks include non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly because the HKMA’s prudential regulation of mortgage lending imposed a cap on banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio for new mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt-servicing burden indicators, but is timelier and can reflect the burden of total outstanding mortgage debt rather than only that of new mortgage debt. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In the short-run equation, the long-run relationship between real private consumption, proxied by average real private consumption per household, and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we use real income, proxied by median household income and deflated by the CCPI; real housing and financial wealth, proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index and deflated by the CCPI; and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total lending continued to increase in the second half of 2017, although growth slowed compared with the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. A sharp shift in global financial market sentiment may also increase fund flow volatility. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly between September and November 2017 and remained near 7.80. This was mainly due to increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management at month-end and ahead of year-end, which tightened liquidity conditions, in turn slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for US dollars increased, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently came under greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. As inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners were minimal and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index (REER), the Hong Kong dollar REER continued to track movements in the NEER closely. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Non-residents’ portfolio investment recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that equity portfolio investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improved economic outlook for the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents’ debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows from residents’ debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that, amid market optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, the survey data indicated that despite a correction in global financial markets, equity investment continued to record inflows, while bond investment recorded modest fund outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalization continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. The possibility that the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered should therefore not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalization and rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in strict accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Fed’s interest rate hikes and continued balance-sheet reduction, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and more recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by a further 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly due to growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the combined total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged in the second half, at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this, the Aggregate Balance decreased, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills totaling HK$80 billion to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management instruments. Entering 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite a correction in the equity market. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply continued to grow in the second half of 2017, although at a slower pace. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Of these, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly because buoyant asset markets increased investment demand. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), but was weighed down by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its asset counterparts On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, growth in US dollar deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits rebounded markedly by 8.4% in the second half after declining continuously for more than two years. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in RMB deposits. Owing to slower growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits, total deposits with authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with 5.6% growth in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management at month-end and ahead of year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, overnight and three-month HIBOR rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December on a monthly-average basis. The negative interest rate differentials between one- to three-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly mirroring movements in the US dollar yield curve. During the second half, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond increased by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates declined in early January. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained broadly stable. Overnight and three-month HIBOR stood at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks’ lending rates increased following a surge in HIBOR, banks’ funding costs generally remained low because of the still-large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage business, banks’ average lending rate for new mortgages gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs, remained soft for most of the second half and stood at 0.38% at the end of December, although it rose briefly in October due to increased funding demand from initial public offerings. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize and other major economies may begin normalizing interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Meanwhile, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase fund flow volatility. However, the large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can serve as a buffer, helping to mitigate an excessively rapid rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window will help curb excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth was as high as 10.2% in the first half, but slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analyzed by currency, amid favorable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Of these, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly because of rising US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total lending recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong, including trade finance, slowed from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Growth in loans for construction, property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities had required banks to strengthen risk management for loans to property developers since June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail sectors declined. By contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related corporate entities remained strong, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans to selected sectors Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other personal purposes, accelerated further to 12.4% in the second half. Strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management customers collateralized by financial assets. Growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such collateralized loans were manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks in January 2014 on risk management for personal loans, requiring them to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers’ debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volume increased, the LTV ratio of newly approved mortgage loans declined, and growth in residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Benefiting mainly from growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After strong credit growth in the first half of 2017, growth moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a notable rise in HIBOR, the cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks remained low because retail deposit rates stayed at low levels. Nevertheless, banks should remain alert to the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows amid the normalization of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of larger-than-expected interest rate increases. To enhance banks’ resilience to system-wide risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% year on year. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down from 1.17% in the first half of 2017 to 1.15% in the second half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017, from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence indicates that the improvement in the net interest margin was consistent with the increase in the average spread on Hong Kong dollar corporate exposures in Hong Kong’s syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans Since September 2017, HIBORs across all tenors have risen, mainly because of liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and banks’ liquidity needs toward year-end, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, three-month HIBOR reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, although it remained relatively low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, HIBOR appeared to stabilize as banks’ year-end liquidity needs subsided. Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, the cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks remained stable. This was mainly attributable to the low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, remained low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was also observed in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks’ average cost of non-deposit market funding in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding cost increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks increased by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The increase in HIBOR exceeded the rise in the overall funding cost of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the interest rate spreads on banks’ HIBOR-based assets. However, this improvement may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have narrowed the spread between their mortgage interest rates and benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. In view of intense competition in the lending market, banks’ net interest margins may come under pressure if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector remained well capitalized. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased from 18.7% at the end of June to 19.1% (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper on proposed rules prescribing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. Although enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions would benefit society by reducing the likelihood of a financial crisis, it would inevitably entail costs. Box 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring a net benefit to the Hong Kong economy. As measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions edged down from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks caused by potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks’ medium- and long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable sources of funding to finance their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the implications of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. It is estimated that, under a hypothetical interest rate shock involving a parallel upward shift of 200 basis points, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Fed will continue raising interest rates and proceed with balance-sheet normalization, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate but still favorable economic environment, growth in the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3% from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of moderating growth, total lending grew solidly by 16.1% in 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of bank loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52%, respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans also declined to 0.54% and 0.4%, respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in recent years of loans for use outside Hong Kong, banks’ asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks As banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit growth, strong credit growth is expected to continue. The HKMA’s December 2017 Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that 29% of respondent authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk from loans to households remained low during the review period. Banks’ mortgage portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at a low level of 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average LTV ratio of newly approved mortgage loans declined further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA introduced the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures in September 2009.

The global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened as persistent trade tensions, tighter financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds increased uncertainty. The Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that decisions would be “data dependent” and that “patience” was needed, prompting investors to rule out the possibility of further interest rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as higher US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Growth in total lending moderated slightly in the second half of 2018, reflecting weaker credit demand amid headwinds such as the continuing China-US trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volume falling markedly and housing prices declining, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds amid heightened uncertainty in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, they could significantly dampen business sentiment and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profits. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact that a potential deterioration in the external environment could have on the credit risk of their related corporate exposures. The global economy continued to grow in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, growth decelerated in Japan and several major Euro area countries, while inflation remained subdued. Slower global trade and a significant decline in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of weakening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth projections for 2019 and 2020 in January by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively from its October 2018 projections. With the growth outlook dimming and trade tensions escalating, global equity markets experienced substantial volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, raising market concerns that the US was approaching a recession. Nevertheless, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term was low. Even so, the global economic outlook remained highly uncertain. In the US, although moderate inflation gave the Fed room to pause its interest rate hikes, the Fed’s data-dependent policy bias also indicated that financial markets could become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as higher US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of the US-China and US-European Union trade negotiations remained uncertain. In the UK, it remained unknown whether a solution to avoid a “hard Brexit” could be achieved. In East Asia, financial markets stabilised as the US dollar’s appreciation slowed and markets expected the Fed to pause its interest rate hikes, but deterioration in the external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade growth momentum had already dragged on economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressure had also eased. Although this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks in balancing support for growth against containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector debt in some regional economies remained severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia was that an unexpected change in the Fed’s monetary policy could produce shocks that spilled over to the sovereign bond markets of emerging market economies, including East Asian economies. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 amid greater uncertainty in the external environment and a slight moderation in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remained uncertain as the China-US trade negotiations had yet to produce an outcome. The significant contraction in shadow financing activities had increased the financing difficulties faced by private corporates, particularly small firms, over the past few quarters, while weakening economic confidence could also put pressure on business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers needed to continue balancing economic stabilisation against the prevention and control of potential system-wide risks by adopting accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted reductions in reserve requirements. Meanwhile, the authorities also adopted more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among firms under different forms of ownership, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0–6.5%. Risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets in 2018. Banks’ asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage of listed non-financial firms edged up. However, banks’ loan impairment charges increased further in the second half of 2018, while their exposures to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments helped protect the banking system against a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage of listed firms in industries with excess capacity—one of the main sources of banks’ credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors contributing to the recent improvement in the business performance of industries with excess capacity. Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stagnated, while year-on-year growth also slowed, bringing full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activity was mainly attributable to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect effects of the China-US trade conflict. Slower growth in private consumption might reflect increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effects arising from corrections in local asset prices. On the external front, Hong Kong’s merchandise export performance also deteriorated, particularly after China and the US imposed additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and explores the short-term outlook and associated risks. Mainly because of slower global economic growth, economic growth was expected to decelerate further in 2019. Given the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance was expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption was expected to continue supporting economic growth amid a low unemployment rate and rising household income, but the outlook for aggregate investment spending could become more uncertain. The Government projected real GDP growth of 2–3% in 2019, while the latest growth projections by private-sector analysts averaged 2.3%. These projections were subject to the many uncertainties and risks discussed above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation partly reflected earlier growth in rentals for newly concluded leases on local private residential properties. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years, total employment growth showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressure was expected to remain moderate in 2019 as local economic growth momentum weakened. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered another four times in March 2019 as of 19 March. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightness. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly because carry trade positions were re-established. Despite the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered again in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion as of 19 March. Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the three-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by about 30 basis points to monthly averages of 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December. Entering 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding cost, rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of September. At the end of January 2019, the average lending rate on new mortgages rose in tandem with the Best Lending Rate to around 2.45%. As uncertainties related to China-US trade tensions and the Brexit negotiations persisted, volatility in fund flows could intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar could stimulate arbitrage activity and lead to fund outflows. Under these circumstances, fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates had faced depreciation pressure amid market concerns about escalating China-US trade tensions. However, buoyed by optimism following the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Although China-US trade tensions persisted, they had not yet had a significant impact on the funding position in the offshore interbank market. Overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily transaction value of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite continuing concerns about China-US trade tensions, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to continue expanding as the Mainland opened its capital account, developed equity and bond market connect schemes, and promoted regional economic cooperation under the Belt and Road initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative. The local equity market experienced roller-coaster-like swings over the past six months. At the beginning of the review period, the market fell sharply because of continued tightening of US monetary policy, major differences between the two sides in the China-US trade negotiations, and growing signs of weakening Mainland economic growth. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the US Fed shifted to a “patient” monetary policy stance. At the same time, during the trade war truce, China adopted further measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the US brought a highly politicised legal case against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides made friendly gestures demonstrating their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this background, the local equity market rallied sharply at the beginning of the year. However, considerable uncertainty remained as the two sides discussed the details of any agreement, while future developments in the US federal government’s prosecution would complicate the situation, particularly in the high-technology sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, and performance improved towards year-end as expectations strengthened that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation would slow. Consequently, flows into bond funds reversed course and increased modestly in the second half. Issuance in Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi market rallied sharply after declining for three consecutive years. However, as Mainland corporates continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remained challenging, and its outlook depended on global economic developments, particularly those in the Mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened under the combined impact of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly outside the United States. In view of the dimmer growth outlook, the Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, stressing that its decisions would be “data dependent” and require “patience,” and ceased providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. As the Fed’s policy inclination becomes data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data and may perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainty over global trade policy and increased geopolitical risks may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since the end of 2018 amid signs that the US interest rate hike cycle was slowing and the US dollar was stabilising. However, as the external environment deteriorates, with the China-US trade conflict remaining unresolved and growth weakening in advanced economies, the region may face a broad-based slowdown. In Mainland China, growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, while uncertainty over the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Accordingly, policymakers introduced more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. In confronting these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and control system-wide risks and supporting corporate entities and the real economy. The global economy continued to grow broadly in the second half of 2018. However, although the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of a slowdown emerged. There were also clear signs that growth momentum outside the United States was weakening. A number of country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emissions standards in Germany, a surge in Italian Central Government bond yields amid the fiscal standoff with the European Union, and social unrest in France—weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp fall in oil prices in the fourth quarter also created new challenges for commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth estimate by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices for selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production in emerging market economies In the fourth quarter, slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, market concerns about the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Fed’s remarks indicating that monetary policy would continue to tighten triggered a sharp correction in global equity markets. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Central Government bond yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry that the United States was approaching a recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Central Government bond yields and the probability of a US recession Nevertheless, the likelihood of a US recession in the near term is very low. US economic fundamentals remain robust, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, and economic overheating is unlikely to prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy sharply. However, possibly taking into account the substantial tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began stressing in early January that monetary policy would be data dependent, noting that moderate inflationary pressure allowed them to remain “patient” when determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the US Federal Open Markets Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes and announced that it “would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments.” This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World ex USA Index, and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Fed’s recent “dovish” signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain and depends on inflation and other developments. Inflationary pressure has so far remained moderate, giving the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary policy normalisation. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that it can “remain patient” (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth outside the United States and trade policy uncertainty. In view of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market- and survey-based indicators of US inflation expectations Nevertheless, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. Under these conditions, wage growth may accelerate, which would normally imply that inflation could intensify in the future (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that essentially ruled out a Fed interest rate hike in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds rate target range remaining unchanged in 2019 and of at least one interest rate hike Overall, a prolonged pause in interest rate hikes by the Fed is not assured. To reduce policy errors, the Fed has increasingly stressed that its decisions will be data dependent as part of its risk-management strategy. This suggests that financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the Euro area, the ECB ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, describing risks to the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside.” The implications of this downgrade to the ECB’s economic growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan stated at its latest policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary easing could be considerable, as its effectiveness has been questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment for a prolonged period have become increasingly evident. For example, regional banks’ capital ratios fell from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from uncertainty surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, uncertainty over the outcomes of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are also two major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. In early December, the US government announced that it would not increase tariffs on goods imported from China for 90 days and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the United States and the European Union have made almost no progress at this stage. Uncertainty over the outcomes of these trade negotiations may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also highly prominent. In the United States, disagreement between the two parties over funding for border security led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives may lead to further policy gridlock. In the United Kingdom, risks associated with Brexit and its repercussions surged after the Theresa May government’s Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and it remains uncertain whether a plan can be formulated at the last minute to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit.” Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as renewed US sanctions on Iran, may also create uncertainty for oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, following repeated volatility during the first three quarters of last year, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter. The US dollar has stabilised since October, while signs that the Fed would remain patient regarding further interest rate hikes have eased currency depreciation and fund outflow pressures facing East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to a net inflow (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency indices and fund flows Despite financial market stability, there are growing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow during the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies—which reflect short-term external trade performance—have fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, foreshadowing a possible further weakening of near-term growth momentum (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers’ Index new export orders indices for East Asian economies Amid slowing growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressure in East Asia has eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline inflation rates and oil prices As recent inflationary pressure and upward pressure on the US dollar have both been relatively moderate, East Asian central banks have no urgent need to raise interest rates, easing the policy dilemma of balancing the promotion of economic growth against the containment of inflation and fund outflows. However, as private-sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging-market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower private consumption growth and weaker export performance amid the China-US trade conflict. With global growth slowing, real GDP growth is also expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the performance of the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressure should remain moderate in 2019, with both upside and downside risks to the outlook. Economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to maintain the strong momentum seen in the first half, and quarter-on-quarter GDP growth turned slightly negative in the second half of the year (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the growth rate at 1.3% in the fourth quarter, below trend growth, bringing full-year growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Calculated on the basis of the expenditure-based, seasonally adjusted volume index of GDP. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component The weakening in economic activity was mainly attributable to the drag on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect effects of the China-US trade conflict. Possibly due to increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect arising from the correction in local asset prices, private consumption growth moderated (Chart 3.1). Gross investment spending declined markedly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after China and the United States implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance in greater detail and explores its short-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms As economic activity weakened, job growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. With weak output and job growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no sign of substantial improvement. As global economic growth slows further, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. In the face of a challenging external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the domestic front, although the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, private consumption growth is expected to slow, partly because of weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect resulting from the earlier correction in asset prices. As for fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. Although building and construction activity is expected to grow steadily as housing supply increases, corporate enterprises may become more cautious about capital investment amid increased economic uncertainty. Business sentiment indicators, such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index, continued to hover in contractionary territory, and forecasts of future economic growth based on the index indicated a further slowdown in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government projected real GDP growth of 2–3% in 2019, while the latest growth estimates by private-sector analysts ranged from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding two chapters. Although local inflationary pressure continued to build in recent months, it remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half of the year. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by rises in certain service prices. Earlier growth in fresh-letting residential rentals and accelerated increases in prices for meals bought away from home continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressure remained broadly moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita payroll Looking ahead, local inflationary pressure should remain moderate in 2019. This mainly reflects weaker domestic growth momentum. However, the earlier increases in private housing rentals will continue to feed through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecast was for a moderate full-year headline inflation rate of 2.2%, while the Government projected an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. Regarding downside risk, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market unexpectedly deteriorates, the currently near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if China-US trade tension eases and the local economy performs better than expected, local inflation could be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The China-US trade conflict gradually intensified in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the United States imposed additional tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China, respectively. Immediately following these two measures, Mainland China responded by imposing additional tariffs of 25% on an equivalent value of US goods. On 24 September, the United States escalated its measures by imposing additional tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing additional tariffs of 5–10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. The two countries subsequently began negotiations to avoid further tariff hikes. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, additional tariffs would inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The China-US trade dispute therefore has important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomy and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and explores its short-term outlook. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify traded goods directly affected by the additional tariffs, thereby examining the impact of the tariff hikes in greater detail. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extracted data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports affected by the successive rounds of additional tariffs described in the preceding section. In the first two rounds of tariff hikes, the United States mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China primarily targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods was broadened to include more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of additional tariffs as List 1, List 2, and List 3, respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focused on year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports to adjust for the effects of seasonality. In addition, caution is required when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity during that month was disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of the additional tariffs. Hong Kong re-exports of Mainland origin affected by tariffs Shortly after the additional tariffs were imposed, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China to the United States through Hong Kong appeared to decline substantially or experience slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 goods slowed in the first month after the additional tariffs were imposed, while re-exports of List 3 goods recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports of all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China to the United States through Hong Kong in 2018 Hong Kong re-exports of US origin affected by tariffs By comparison, goods re-exported from the United States to Mainland China through Hong Kong showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports of List 1 goods appeared to decline substantially in the months following the tariff hikes, but recovered towards the end of the year. Re-exports of List 2 goods generally recorded negative growth throughout the year, while growth in List 3 goods appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the United States to Mainland China through Hong Kong in 2018 Front-loading As there was a time lag between the announcement and eventual implementation of the tariffs—or simply because of the threat of tariff hikes—corporate enterprises might increase shipments of affected goods before the anticipated effective dates of the tariffs. Indeed, some information and news reports indicated that such front-loading behaviour was fairly widespread. Some private-sector analysts also considered such behaviour to be partly responsible for the strong headline trade figures before the tariff hikes. The more granular trade data showed some signs of front-loading for goods on certain tariff lists, but this appeared to involve only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the United States (Chart B3.1). Growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 goods increased in the months before their respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, growth in goods re-exported from the United States to Mainland China through Hong Kong (Chart B3.2) showed no clear evidence of front-loading by corporate enterprises. Hong Kong re-exports unaffected by additional tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the additional tariffs accounted for only around 4–5% of the total value of Hong Kong’s re-exports. To obtain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs should also be examined. We found that re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in both of the final two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Moreover, growth in tariff-affected re-exports (red line) declined much more sharply from the third quarter onwards, indicating that the tariffs had a significant impact. The slowdown in re-exports unaffected by additional tariffs partly reflected broader weakness in external demand. As persistent trade tension continues to increase uncertainty, global financial conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks rise, external demand may come under more widespread pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in corrections in major equity markets. Import demand from other economies was consequently dampened, constraining Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Global growth is likely to slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators showed that corporate enterprises of all sizes were pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trading sector particularly subdued. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightness driven by anticipated seasonal funding demand. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly because corporate entities repatriated proceeds raised through initial public offerings and the market rebuilt carry-trade positions, triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before falling back in January 2019. Looking ahead, uncertainties arising from the continuing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization may result in greater volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, carry-trade activity may continue, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which would be consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four more times in March 2019 (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightness, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilized again after November, as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity and led to the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting the repatriation by corporate entities of proceeds raised through initial public offerings and the rebuilding of carry-trade positions in the market. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken gradually and triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance had remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), before declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March (as of 19 March). Hong Kong dollar fund outflows since April 2018 accounted for only a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion that had flowed in since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation rate differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the latter broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER The latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased equity-market volatility, outflows of local residents’ equity securities investment accelerated, more than offsetting inflows of non-residents’ portfolio investment in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both local residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, uncertainties arising from the continuing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization may intensify volatility in fund flows.
