In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate arbitrage activity, leading to fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and could trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again. Fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are both part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the continuing normalization of US interest rates and the repeated triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking between April and August, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year to HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base mainly reflected the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while certificates of indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for the broader measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply, money-supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainty in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year but increased only slightly, by 0.1%, in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits were little changed from the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly because of fewer investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth following increases in deposit rates. An analysis of counterpart assets showed that the slowdown in Hong Kong dollar M3 growth was attributable to changes in banks’ capital and reserves, which were included under “net other items.” Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets Growth in foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half of the year. Following increases in banks’ preferential US dollar deposit rates, the resulting growth in deposits caused US dollar deposits to rise strongly by 8.8% in the second half, making them the main driver of growth in foreign currency deposits (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Despite the still-large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposit base, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank rates, making them more volatile than longer-term interbank rates (Chart 4.7). Three-month and 12-month HIBOR averaged 2.32% and 2.74%, respectively, in December, around 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Entering 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The averages for three-month and 12-month HIBOR fell to 1.65% and 2.39%, respectively, in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, the yields on three-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points, respectively, to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average lending rate for new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in the cost of interbank and deposit funding, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before falling back to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of rising funding costs, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September. However, retail banks did not adjust their Best Lending Rates again after the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised once more in December. Meanwhile, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose in line with the Best Lending Rate to around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the US dollar interest rate trajectory, fund flows, and local financial-market activity, such as initial public offering subscriptions, will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial volume of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, which banks may use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increases in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating China-US trade tensions, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened against the US dollar from the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilized in November amid optimism generated by the resumption of high-level China-US trade negotiations. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates To date, the continuing China-US trade tensions have not had a significant impact on the funding position in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally because of seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). Three-month CNH HIBOR hovered at around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting the monetary easing measures recently introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of developments in China-US trade negotiations on liquidity in the CNH interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixing Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was driven mainly by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit declined by a further 14.1% in the second half, mainly because fewer certificates of deposit were issued and a relatively large volume matured in October.

Benefiting mainly from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Their capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting the upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank rates and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, retail banks’ overall Hong Kong dollar funding cost rose markedly, although it remained at a relatively low level. Amid uncertainties in the external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilizing from November onwards, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from persistent uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations, the global economic slowdown, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the impact that a possible further deterioration in the external environment could have on the credit risk of their related corporate exposures. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while their return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly attributable to substantial growth in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 19.4%, while their return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period a year earlier (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and the decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to compete for stable long-term funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. In addition, following the US interest rate hike decision in late September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the increases in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, although it remained low by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upwards. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost rose by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half of the year (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks and term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates The cumulative increase in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate exceeded the rise in the overall funding cost of Hong Kong banks, which may have had a positive impact on retail banks’ HIBOR-based mortgages, a type of loan that the industry had actively promoted over the preceding few years. However, further improvement in the net interest margin may become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgages have already reached their Best Lending Rate-based caps. As the timing of future increases in the Best Lending Rate remains uncertain, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid the normalization of US interest rates may weigh on the overall net interest margin. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment may cloud banks’ profitability outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, persistent uncertainty surrounding China-US trade relations may dampen business sentiment and reduce demand for bank credit. If this results in a significant decline in lending and deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on bank profitability. The Hong Kong banking sector remained strongly capitalized, well above the international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated AIs rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Since 1 January 2013, locally incorporated AIs have been required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Accordingly, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a sound level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs As measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, likewise well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. As one of the Basel III liquidity standards, the Net Stable Funding Ratio indicated that the funding position of AIs was stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained high at 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of AIs indicated that the Hong Kong banking sector was capable of withstanding a variety of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for AIs, reflecting the stable funding structure maintained by the banking system. At the end of 2018, customer deposits as a proportion of the total liabilities of all AIs edged up from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs 1. Figures may not add up to the total owing to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs fell from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, as Hong Kong dollar deposits grew much more slowly than Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks decreased slightly in the second half of 2018. It was estimated that, under a hypothetical parallel interest rate shock of 200 basis points, the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks could decline by an amount equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11 Impact of interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks 1. Interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard parallel interest rate shock of 200 basis points on institutions’ interest rate risk exposures. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainty arising from the China-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed markedly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilizing from November 2018 onwards. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all AIs declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic loans, including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing, and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Growth in domestic loans slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2%, respectively, in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, growth in total lending slowed markedly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand is likely to remain weak in the near term. The HKMA’s December 2018 Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that, among all surveyed AIs, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of AIs expecting demand to decline rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite the slight decline in total lending in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of the bank loan portfolio remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs edged down to 0.55% and 0.36%, respectively, at the end of December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40%, respectively, at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio decreased slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks 1. Classified loans refer to loans classified as “substandard”, “doubtful”, or “loss”. 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of the Hong Kong offices and overseas branches of retail banks. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include the major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks. On a half-yearly basis, growth in loans to households slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly attributable to slower growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes, which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal GDP grew more slowly than loans to households, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak since early 2020 has simultaneously hit demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic impact of the outbreak, financial markets remain volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance staying stable and total deposits growing moderately, no noticeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the banking system in Hong Kong were observed during the review period. After a moderate rally in the first half of 2019, growth in total lending slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market generally softened from mid-2019, although its movements were somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increases in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth had shown preliminary signs of stabilisation, supported by stepped-up monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of China-US trade tensions and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit” in the United Kingdom. However, the continued increase in coronavirus infections worldwide since late January has raised market concerns and triggered sharp volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks of the outbreak, several major central banks substantially cut interest rates and expanded their liquidity facilities, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp declines in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will weigh on global economic activity, and the extent of its economic impact will depend on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, tensions between the United States and its major trading partners may intensify again, while post-Brexit trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union may also encounter significant difficulties. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 The region’s exports to major destinations, including the United States, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but whether there will be a broad-based rally in the technology product cycle remains to be seen. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One China-US trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce reduced uncertainty surrounding global trade to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region’s economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel restrictions imposed by several economies in the region may hurt Asia’s tourism industry, particularly economies that are more reliant on exports of tourism services. Given the region’s close supply-chain links with Mainland China, manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 owing to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One China-US trade agreement will help temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressure remains amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made economic stabilisation a priority for 2020 while also emphasising the containment of financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have suggested that private industrial enterprises may have experienced declines in equity in recent years, which has been viewed as a sign of a “private-sector retreat”. Using 2018 data on listed firms, Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in the equity of Mainland industrial enterprises and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. Although the study finds that negative profits are the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural factors, also warrant attention (see Box 2 for details). Local economic activity contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main drag on GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, weakening the economic outlook and in turn dampening consumer and corporate business sentiment. With the renewed escalation of China-US trade tensions, slowing global economic growth and the severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued. Given the severe headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater scope to step up support for the local economy and help moderate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity for corporates, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent outbreak also posing substantial downside risks. As industries such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism and transportation have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these industries. However, the package of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and corporates, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to corporates with a 100% Government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.2 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, giving banks greater scope to step up support for the local economy, particularly industries and individuals facing greater short-term pressure because of the outbreak. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak owing to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slightly positive impact on the local economy in the short term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activity, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government projects real GDP growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks arising from slowing global economic growth, China-US trade relations, Mainland China’s economic performance and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate will rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 provides a more detailed discussion of recent labour-market developments and the short-term outlook. Local inflationary pressure continued to build through the third quarter of 2019, mainly because of increases in fresh pork prices; inflation momentum subsequently eased gradually as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to moderate in the near term amid weak economic conditions, consolidating private housing rentals and moderate imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts for the headline inflation rate in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government projects underlying inflation of 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including demand associated with initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly because of buoyant initial public offering activity and partly because year-end liquidity tightness prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, without triggering the Convertibility Undertaking. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at approximately HK$54 billion. Short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have fluctuated since the fourth quarter of 2019, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital-market activity such as initial public offerings. Box 4 examines how market attention to future initial public offering activity affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest-rate caps linked to the Best Lending Rate, the average lending rate on new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October. However, as Best Lending Rates in the market were lowered from November, the average lending rate on new mortgages edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance staying stable and total deposits growing moderately, no noticeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the banking system in Hong Kong were observed during the review period. Nevertheless, it is necessary to monitor the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus outbreak amid uncertainty in the external environment. With its substantial foreign reserves position and sound banking system, Hong Kong has the capability, resources and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability. During the review period, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened on market expectations of a China-US trade agreement, but came under weakening pressure following the coronavirus outbreak from late January 2020. In the latter part of 2019, offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to onshore renminbi. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the differential remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool recovered slightly after a modest decline during the previous review period. At the end of January 2020, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion. Hong Kong’s other renminbi businesses also expanded, with strong growth recorded in local renminbi bank loans and renminbi trade settlement. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion for 2019 as a whole. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, increased allocation to renminbi assets by international investors, and deeper regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilising, raising market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, the continued increase in global coronavirus infections since late January 2020 dashed hopes of a recovery and deepened investor concerns about a global economic downturn, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To address the economic shock, major central banks and some governments introduced stimulus measures from early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 clouded the outlook for regional economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism industry being particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 because of weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States should temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressure remains amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities’ monetary and fiscal policy responses will provide some buffer. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was still sluggish in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilising in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier policy easing by the Fed and the ECB, as well as an easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US “Phase One” trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index However, the continued increase in global coronavirus infections since the end of January and the ensuing economic shock raised market concerns and triggered a wave of selling in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in the global supply chain, disruptions to production activity in the Mainland and the resulting drag on its economic growth will generate significant spillovers that could spread worldwide (Chart 2.3). Since late February, coronavirus infections have surged outside Mainland China, potentially exacerbating supply chain disruptions and creating a risk of directly weighing on domestic economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index option-adjusted spread Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) In response to the potentially severe economic shock caused by the epidemic, some central banks, including the Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, cut interest rates from early March, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support households and corporates. However, financial markets continued to face enormous selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which could in turn intensify downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economy Financial Conditions Index Apart from developments in the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks declined following the China-US Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations could be fraught with difficulties because many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom are not expected to proceed smoothly, prolonging post-Brexit uncertainty. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 because of subdued global demand. East Asia’s exports to major destinations, including the United States, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although preliminary signs suggested that the downturn in regional technology products was bottoming out, including reports by major regional electronics companies of improved profits at the end of 2019,6 whether regional technology exports have staged a substantive rally remains to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainty also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region’s potential economic growth over the longer term. To support economic growth amid moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting them in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak raised concerns that regional economies could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As several regional economies imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry bore the brunt, particularly in economies that rely more heavily on visitors from Mainland China and exports of travel services (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and worsening epidemic would also affect regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese tourists In the short term, the epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Based on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects could be temporary, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and geographical spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government action to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations indicate that corporate earnings will deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged the search for yield, thereby pushing up asset prices without support from fundamentals. As a result, regional equity markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of benchmark equity index constituents Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth could make it more difficult for the region’s private sector to repay debt. Although lower domestic interest rates may provide breathing room for indebted corporates and households, they could also sow the seeds of further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, when more index-tracking capital flows into regional financial markets, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector may also intensify, although this effect may be confined to corporates with stronger financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, in terms of external factors, East Asian economies may face increased risks from an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress on the China-US Phase One trade agreement, trade tensions between the two countries persist because the fundamental trade issues between them remain unresolved. As evidenced by the growing trade surpluses of several regional economies with the United States (Chart 2.9), multinational companies seeking to avoid tariffs may continue to look for additional sources of supply outside China-centred supply chains. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging market economies, excluding China, with the United States had risen to approximately US$167 billion. If their trade surpluses with the United States continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies could become the next targets of the trade conflict; for example, in July 2019 the US government imposed punitive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam.7 In view of this, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain despite the China-US trade truce. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surplus with the United States Over the past decade, increasing integration of international financial markets has led to a significant rise in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study showed that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows were driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices, commonly known as passive funds, but also actively managed funds that use investment indices as references.9 By bringing in overseas investors that the economies concerned would otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Such funds therefore diversify the investor base of emerging market economies, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are market concerns that their investments may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby leading to high levels of corporate leverage.10 In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated volatility in global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, more vulnerable.11 This box assesses the implications of index-driven investment for financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to constituent bonds according to each bond’s weight in the benchmark index. Compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may therefore give issuers of index constituent bonds less incentive to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and debt servicing ability risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of corporates from each emerging market economy in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for investment in their bonds by passive bond funds,14 we find that increased investment of this kind raises the long-term, rather than short-term, leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the broader long-term bond investor base provided by passive bond funds also supports the development of corporates in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effect is significant only for corporates in emerging market economies with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with greater debt servicing ability and lower leverage ratios (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher costs of financial distress, corporates with high leverage or weaker debt servicing ability instead appear unlikely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of investment by passive bond funds. Overall, the above findings suggest that growth in passive bond fund investment may not substantially increase debt servicing ability risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending and poor export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, while the recent coronavirus outbreak has also brought significant downside risk. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China–US trade relations, economic performance in Mainland China and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease, although its outlook is subject to potential upside and downside risks. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP declined successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, while the resulting deterioration in the economic outlook undermined consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract markedly from the third quarter onwards.33 Amid heightened economic uncertainties and worsening business sentiment, gross investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter.34 On the external front, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued amid escalating China–US trade tensions, weaker global economic growth and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Chart 3.2).35 As export of services contracted sharply, net trade dragged down GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Given the enormous headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment and support corporates, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely affected sectors such as retail, food services, transport and the tourism industry.36 To give banks greater scope to step up support for the local economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would lower the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity for corporates, including SMEs. Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, while the recent outbreak has also brought significant downside risk. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, the series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and corporates, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to corporates with a 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.37 The HKMA’s further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks greater scope to step up support for the local economy, especially sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure as a result of the outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak owing to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the China–US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activity, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government projects real GDP growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). In particular, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of the social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was concentrated mainly in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges, and the unemployment rate is highly likely to rise further. Box 3 examines in greater detail recent labour market developments and the short-term outlook. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressure continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to rising fresh pork prices; as economic activity subsequently weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the increase eased slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was attributable to reduced price pressure across a number of CPI components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained pronounced because of rising fresh pork prices, although price pressure on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and on durable goods remained moderate. For services, as growth in earlier fresh-letting residential rental slowed, growth in the CPI rental component also trended downwards (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressure increased slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressure is expected to ease in the short term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private housing rental continues to slow, the housing rental component of inflation should moderate further. On the external front, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2020 ranges from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government projects an underlying inflation rate of 2.5% and a headline inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe-than-expected economic deterioration, for example because of a prolonged coronavirus outbreak, could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, more severe disruptions to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents continued that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% at the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this background, this box analyses recent labour market developments and the short-term outlook, including why overall labour market conditions remained broadly resilient during the first three quarters of 2019, with the unemployment rate virtually unchanged, and the implications for future developments. It also examines some risk factors that could cause the unemployment rate to rise sharply. It should be noted that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year real GDP growth rate by around two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagged nature may explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth and the unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China–US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt severe blows to employment in the trade sector and in the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors continued to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the finance, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained resilient, while financial activities relating to fintech development and initial public offerings were also highly active. These factors may have helped support the job market in the financial and business services sectors. Moreover, public administration, social and personal services, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appeared less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that although employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, public administration, social and personal services respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even when the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against an increase in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand- and supply-side factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 Meanwhile, the increase in employment during the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted markedly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment declined during the economic downturn, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some changes in the structure of the labour market are also noteworthy. In particular, the increased share of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the shares of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment have declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, making them the second-largest group in total employment, at around 7% in 2017.42 Companies may therefore retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours at present, partly reflecting the greater prevalence of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum increasing further in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range in recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly attributable to equity-related demand and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by year-end liquidity tightness. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. Although coronavirus-related shifts in market sentiment amid an uncertain external environment could lead to heightened fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong’s substantial foreign reserves position and robust banking system enable it to withstand fund outflow pressures without compromising local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for Hong Kong dollars, including demand from initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October onwards (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar increased further, and from mid-December through February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant IPO activity and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by year-end liquidity tightness. After the Lunar New Year holiday, the liquidity position eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and therefore had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, movements in the real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked those in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER When measuring fund flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinctly different but interrelated concepts: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through the banking system in Hong Kong, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong’s overall financial system. The two fund-flow concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert large amounts of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for Hong Kong dollars will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, resulting in a reduction in the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, while the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range in recent months. Therefore, no significant outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, the total deposits in Hong Kong’s banking system are a useful indicator. If substantial funds flow out of Hong Kong’s banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no significant cross-border fund outflows. Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly, indicating that the coronavirus outbreak had thus far had only a limited impact on the local monetary environment. Nevertheless, the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak need to be closely monitored. With its substantial foreign reserves position and robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to address fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, increasing by 4.0% from end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. The other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators remained broadly stable. Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) increased by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and then edged up by 0.2% during the seven months from the end of June 2019. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that the increase in Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and a rise in the Monetary Base, driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). During the seven months since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar deposits, the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its asset counterparts During the seven months since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with RMB deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions have increased steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s total broad money supply also grew at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5%, respectively, since the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate because of various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand and business- and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, as IPO activity in the Hong Kong equity market became more active, the overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced relatively large fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally increased. Subscriptions for large IPOs can exert significant pressure on overnight rates. The empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to future IPO activity can also affect the three-month HIBOR. This may occur when market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines of large IPOs and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average new-mortgage lending rate At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. The increase mainly reflected banks’ continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, resulting in a rise in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the lowering of the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of October 2019, several retail banks reduced their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgages benchmarked against HIBOR, major banks raised the interest-rate caps determined with reference to the Best Lending Rate, causing the average new-mortgage lending rate to rise to around 2.63% in October. 45 Following reductions in market Best Lending Rates since November, the average mortgage rate declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the US Fed in achieving its policy objectives, the US Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March and 15 March (US time). Although HIBOR tracks movements in US interest rates over the long term, short-term HIBOR may be affected by local factors that influence demand for Hong Kong dollars, such as local IPO activity. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, HIBOR may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply and demand of Hong Kong dollar funding. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightness, banks may use the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid concerns that the China-US trade conflict might intensify, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations that China and the United States would resume trade negotiations reversed the weakening trend of the renminbi. The offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly moved beyond 6.9 in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States. However, since the end of January, the offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced weakening pressure because of the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore renminbi traded mostly at a discount to the onshore renminbi from May to August, but broadly at a premium later in 2019. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, although the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November because of MSCI A-share rebalancing, and at the end of January 2020 ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday.

Amid increased uncertainty in the global and local economic environment, the profitability of Hong Kong retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and sound by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although growth in total lending slowed in the second half of last year, it continued to outpace deposit growth during the review period. Accordingly, both the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose. However, given the stable level of the Aggregate Balance in the banking system and broadly steady deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increase in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit59 of retail banks edged down by 1.5% from the same period in 2018. Accordingly, return on assets dipped to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the corresponding period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses at retail banks led to a slight decline in profit. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Although the US Fed Funds target rate was cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, no significant downward pressure has yet emerged in the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market. Instead, influenced by a number of local factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market, shorter-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term, stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate, an indicator of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose gradually from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained low by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in the US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding cost, their average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding cost and the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank rates, supporting banking sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local framework for interest rate risk in the banking book have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. Overall funding costs and maturities were calculated as weighted averages of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onward are not directly comparable with those for earlier months. Looking ahead, various downside risk factors in the external and local environments will continue to cloud the profitability outlook for banks. These include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of China-US trade relations and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could weaken the already sluggish momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment may persist, potentially putting pressure on banks’ future net interest margins. Locally, the social incidents that began in mid-2019 continue to weigh on business investment and business confidence. Against an already weak economic backdrop, if the situation persists or deteriorates further, the outlook for credit demand and banks’ asset quality could worsen. In terms of overall market developments, following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s granting of eight virtual bank licences, the Hong Kong banking sector began rolling out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market shares by attracting new customers with more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate because the current scale of virtual banks’ operations is still limited, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate their adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results of Box 5 show that the extent of financial technology adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically associated with improvements in cost efficiency and higher profitability. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standard. At the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III imposes a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions As measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio65 requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio,66 one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated that the funding position of authorized institutions was stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained high at 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%.
