The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained high at 134.5%, also above the applicable statutory minimum requirement of 75% for 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding a variety of liquidity shocks. At the end of 2019, customer deposits as a share of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Overall, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the year. Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system had remained stable since April 2019 and deposits were broadly steady, there were no clear signs of significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the banking system in Hong Kong during the review period. It is estimated that, under a hypothetical interest rate shock of a 200-basis-point rise in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would decline by an amount equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11). On a half-yearly basis, loan growth, as measured by changes in the total amount of loans and advances of all authorized institutions, rose moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019 before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was attributable to weaker growth during the review period in both domestic loans, including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively, in the second half of 2019, lower than their respective growth rates of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, growth in total lending for 2019 as a whole increased moderately to 6.7%, compared with 4.4% for 2018 as a whole.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hope of reopening economies and boosted the global growth outlook. Together with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, this drove financial markets to successive record highs. However, the global outlook remained shrouded in uncertainty, and the pace of recovery was expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the lasting economic scarring caused by the pandemic would pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money market continued to operate smoothly and orderly. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand due to recurring waves of the pandemic, total lending by the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, although it still recorded a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainty over the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks would continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic could weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant regarding the impact of the related downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rallied in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but the renewed rise in COVID-19 infections from the fourth quarter caused global growth to slow again. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end, facilitating a return of the global economy to normality and accelerating growth. Together with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, this pushed global financial markets to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainty would continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remained to be seen whether vaccines could be distributed widely. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could cause inflation to exceed expectations, in turn requiring central banks to scale back monetary easing earlier and bringing an end to financial markets’ expectations of a “lower for longer” monetary policy. Over the longer term, policymakers would need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt and lasting economic scarring. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded and the search for yield re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia continued to face persistent uncertainty arising from the pandemic. First, amid global competition for vaccine procurement, the region’s less-developed economies might lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage or effectiveness, together with weakened fiscal positions among governments in the region, could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. In Mainland China, the economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activity gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook would still depend heavily on developments in the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecast indicated that the Mainland economy would grow by 8.4% in 2021. The RMB weakened for several months at the beginning of 2020, but strengthened during the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened and the Mainland bond market recorded strong capital inflows. A detailed study showed that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Box 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level. With a slight increase in domestic demand and further expansion in merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first-ever decline for two consecutive years. The latest sectoral GDP data showed that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely during the pandemic than the overall economy. In response to the prolonged pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds—the third and fourth rounds—of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and strengthen Hong Kong’s capacity to combat it. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including issuing a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and providing unemployed persons with special 100%-guaranteed personal loans. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade financing facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the liquidity difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines offered hope that economic activity could return to normal, and the local economy was expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery would be affected by numerous uncertainties, including developments in the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government projected real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% in 2021, while the growth estimates of international institutions and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, its highest level since the SARS outbreak. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressure continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation fell markedly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and declined further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, an indicator of inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. As global and local economic conditions remained challenging, inflationary pressure in Hong Kong was likely to remain mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation would continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in growth in fresh-letting residential rentals. The market consensus forecast put the headline inflation rate for 2021 at a moderate 1.4%, while the Government projected underlying and headline inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including demand arising from buoyant initial public offering activity and southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activity remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. An analysis by geographical location showed that total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties relating to developments in the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions could increase fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong had ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, and was therefore capable of withstanding volatility in fund flows. As the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. As funding costs declined, the average new-mortgage lending rate also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Alongside the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. During most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium to the CNY exchange rate. The average premium in the fourth quarter was around 100 pips, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit rising to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi businesses, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-boundary fund-flow channels linking to the Mainland. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, increasing demand among international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative. Supported by rising global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong equities by Mainland investors through Southbound Stock Connect, the local equity market rallied after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose for several reasons, including the unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery in economic activity; and reduced global geopolitical uncertainty. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its sharp decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and briefly surpassing the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and CNH debt markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following significant net outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered rapidly as governments around the world introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in inflows into local bond funds. Although bond yields rallied moderately over the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained close to historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development raising market expectations that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually end and global economic growth would subsequently accelerate, and amid expectations of “lower for longer” global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the financial markets’ buoyant expectations were disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. If the economic recovery proved weaker than expected, or policy support was withdrawn earlier than anticipated—for example, because inflation exceeded expectations—asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support, as well as how to address the many legacies of the pandemic, including high debt levels and lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continued to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, while the region’s less-developed emerging market economies could face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in vaccination programmes could reverse the prevailing optimism and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remained highly uncertain and would depend largely on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The Government therefore announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of containing system-wide risk. Benefiting from the release of pent-up purchasing power following economic re-opening, most major economies recorded stronger-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, COVID-19 infections began to rise again in the fourth quarter, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social-distancing measures and weakening global growth momentum once more. More transmissible variants emerged at the end of 2020 and subsequently spread around the world, further exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines at the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end and the global economy would return to normal and grow more rapidly. Another force supporting the global economic recovery came from ongoing policy stimulus measures, including major central banks’ commitments to “lower for longer” monetary policy amid subdued inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing by major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund raised its projection for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage point higher than its October 2020 projection (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth projections by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices in cyclical sectors, which typically benefit from an economic recovery, rose, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 Twelve-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major equity indices However, while financial markets performed strongly, macroeconomic conditions remained challenging. This disconnect could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control depended on whether vaccines could be distributed widely, which remained to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX promoted more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supplies were expected to make persistently low vaccination rates an even more serious problem in lower-income emerging market economies. If the pandemic was not brought under control as expected, social-distancing and other restrictive measures might have to be extended, thereby undermining the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Share of the population in selected economies that had received at least one vaccine dose (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the financial-market rally was founded on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly “lower for longer” monetary policy. However, there was a risk that support measures could be withdrawn more quickly than expected. For example, amid the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe had already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation proved stronger than expected, central banks might need to scale back their policy-easing plans, while higher-than-expected inflation data could also increase financial-market volatility. Chart 2.4 US and Euro-area five-year/five-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, significant uncertainty surrounded future China-US relations. The trend towards China-US “decoupling”, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, had intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance towards Mainland China among both Democrats and Republicans in the US, this trend might not be reversed under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger financial-market turmoil. Looking ahead, policymakers would need to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. Although withdrawing these measures too early could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a “cliff effect”, the measures would be costly in the long run, including by imposing fiscal burdens and delaying the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources—for example, by allowing “zombie corporates” with no longer viable business models to survive through continued government support. In addition, policymakers would need to address the many problems left behind by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 because of falling corporate income and surging government expenditure (Chart 2.5). Although the problems caused by the sharp increase in debt might not be imminent because global interest rates were currently extremely low, continued debt accumulation in the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt as a percentage of GDP Another legacy concerned the long-term economic losses or lasting scarring that could result from the pandemic. For example, persistently high uncertainty could cause corporates to reduce investment, while workers suffering from prolonged unemployment might permanently leave the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after falling sharply in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was driven mainly by a rebound in exports, with particularly strong export demand for electronics and technological equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers, remained under severe strain. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite continued uncertainty surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment capital had resumed flowing into the region. Since the second half of the previous year, improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced-economy bonds had attracted more bond capital inflows into the region (Chart 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production programmes were launched, equity capital inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly amid portfolio capital inflows, enabling the Bloomberg-JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rally by about 10% from its low in March of the previous year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment fund flows East Asia continued to face persistent uncertainty surrounding the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines brought hope to the region’s hardest-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early vaccine supplies drove up procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also posed challenges to the region’s logistics and public-health capabilities. As a result, the region’s less-developed economies might achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, while uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related sectors. Second, as investor optimism was driven largely by vaccine rollouts, the current capital inflows and rally in financial asset prices could end if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination fell far short of expectations. An abrupt decline in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports also continued to grow, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-tech products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, Mainland China’s GDP still grew by 2.3% despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions of demand components to GDP growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicated that the Mainland economy would grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery could be sustained would still depend to some extent on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland had normalised, service sectors remained partially disrupted following renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although export growth resumed in the second half of 2020, global demand remained uncertain because of renewed outbreaks in most advanced economies. In addition, China-US tensions might not ease in the near term. However, the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the agreed EU-China Comprehensive Agreement on Investment would facilitate Mainland China’s further integration with other economies and could partially offset the adverse effects of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Given the continued uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, the Government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that there would be no major change in the existing policy stance in 2021, in order to support economic growth. At the same time, it emphasised the importance of containing system-wide risk, including by maintaining stable macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identified technological self-reliance and self-strengthening and dual circulation as development priorities, with a view to raising per capita GDP to the level of a moderately developed economy by 2035. The COVID-19 outbreak appeared to have had only a limited impact on the repayment capability of bond-issuing corporates, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained low in the second half of 2020. However, the total value of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 because of a sharp rise in defaults on bonds issued by state-owned enterprises (Chart 2.9). Although the rise in SOE defaults mainly reflected the Central Government’s determination to break implicit guarantees for SOEs and promote more rational market pricing of risk, limited fiscal space among some local governments, particularly those in less-developed regions, might also have been a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Scale and ratio of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, funding costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the ongoing economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to higher funding costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: Five-year corporate bond yields In the property market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities rose much more slowly (Chart 2.11). The housing oversupply that had troubled third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below its peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as local demand recovered and merchandise exports expanded further. With hopes that COVID-19 vaccination would enable economic activity to return to normal, the local economy was expected to resume growth in 2021 after recording its most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine roll-outs. As widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would continue to face considerable challenges in early 2021. The labour market was therefore expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressure would remain mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below its pre-pandemic level. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first two consecutive years of decline in history. The latest GDP data for different industries also showed that economic activity in the vast majority of industries recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with contractions in consumption- and tourism-related industries more severe than that in the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover in the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters. However, consumer confidence remained weak as the authorities reimposed social-distancing measures amid the third and fourth local waves of the pandemic. Overall investment spending also grew in the second half of the year as business sentiment briefly improved. Benefiting partly from stronger export performance, particularly exports to Mainland China, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as the global tourism industry remained at a standstill. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting the slower recovery in merchandise exports than in imports. In the recent 2021/22 Budget, the Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy, including a one-off HKD5,000 electronic Consumption Voucher Scheme and 100% government-guaranteed personal concessionary loans for unemployed persons. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced a further extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October that year and an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines were expected to enable economic activity to return to normal, and the Hong Kong economy was projected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine roll-outs. As widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would continue to face considerable challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government projected real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, the highest level in 17 years (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while government figures showed a continued decline in the number of job vacancies. The nominal index of payroll per person engaged, which reflects labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest growth rate in nearly 11 years. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Local inflationary pressure continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation fell markedly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. Specifically, price pressure on basic food items eased, while the cost of meals bought away from home declined noticeably, reflecting the takeaway discounts offered by more restaurants while dine-in services were restricted. Price pressure on other tradable goods, such as durable goods, remained moderate. On the services front, the CCPI rental component remained weak as private housing rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressure also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6).
