In particular, local inflation would continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in fresh-letting residential rental growth. The market consensus forecast put the headline inflation rate for 2021 at a moderate 1.4%, while the Government projected underlying inflation of 1% and a headline inflation rate of 1.6% for 2021. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism rapidly plunged into a depression, raising market concerns that the crisis would have scarring effects on the subsequent labour market recovery. Against this background, this box empirically analyses the impact of the inbound tourism boom on Hong Kong’s labour market to explore the potential implications of the current tourism slump. Inbound tourism has experienced dramatic ups and downs since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the 2003 outbreak of SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome). Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July that year, visitor arrivals began to surge. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply as individuals to visit Hong Kong once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry Individual Visit Endorsements for visits to Hong Kong within one year. The number of Mainland visitors has risen substantially since then. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure links with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached record highs from late 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, while inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Using the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We regard the introduction of the IVS in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock because its timing was nearly exogenous and its introduction was unforeseeable to Hong Kong residents. The main data for our analysis come from population data in Hong Kong’s Population Censuses or By-censuses. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. We also define tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hotel and transport industries. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences analytical framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after implementation of the IVS between younger workers aged 20–40 in the “treatment group” and older workers aged 41–65 in the “comparison group”. We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can therefore make major changes to their employment choices more flexibly in response to exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market may change over time, we also use an event study to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers—especially women and workers with only secondary education—were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after implementation of the IVS. In particular, the IVS had a notably significant and persistent impact on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries, remaining close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards in terms of the average difference in the probability of entering such industries relative to the older cohort (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare the earnings of workers in tourism-related industries, the treatment group, with those in non-tourism-related industries, the comparison group. The estimates show that after implementation of the IVS, earnings growth among workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that among employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and less-educated workers in tourism-related industries recorded larger and rising earnings gains of 3–20 percentage points (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the earnings of female and less-educated workers The above findings are broadly consistent with international experience, showing that the tourism industry is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and less-educated workers. In Hong Kong’s case, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses that strong growth in inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the labour market for the lower-skilled segment. As inbound tourism has fallen from boom to trough, these groups of workers may be more severely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, with the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to more than HK$450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. Although uncertainties surrounding the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may intensify volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand pressures arising from fund-flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some IPO proceeds were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505–7.7544 in November and December amid improving sentiment in the local equity market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards year-end. With fundraising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, repeated triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking led to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at end-August to HK$457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicated no signs of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance-of-payments figures showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual fund movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index broadly declined in tandem with the US dollar’s weakening against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may intensify volatility in fund flows. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities, such as IPOs, thereby generating substantial fund inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fundraising activities may attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, proceeds raised by listed firms may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand volatility in fund flows without affecting financial stability. Amid continued fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the increase in the Aggregate Balance arising from the repeated triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. Meanwhile, the other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large IPOs increased Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, resulting in notable increases in Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As the IPOs were completed and customers repaid their IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. In January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 rose sharply again, mainly driven by a large IPO at the end of the month. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7% over the seven months since end-June; excluding the impact of the IPO at end-January, it grew moderately by 9.1%. According to the analysis of counterpart assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the expansion of the Monetary Base resulting from the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of the IPO at end-January, they grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined because of low deposit rates, this was more than fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since end-June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, owing to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits with authorized institutions increased markedly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO at end-January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate because of various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand and business- and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. As the Aggregate Balance increased, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large IPOs in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not fluctuate significantly because of ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points over the same period to 1.30%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average new-mortgage lending rate Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level mainly declined in tandem with HIBORs. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). With lower funding costs, the average new-mortgage lending rate also declined from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking one-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given that US interest rates are expected to remain low for an extended period, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should also remain low, with occasional fluctuations arising from capital-market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the banking system’s ample liquidity should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar have strengthened since end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook for Mainland China relative to the rest of the world and the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell’s announcement at end-September that Mainland Central Government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index further supported the strengthening of the renminbi through investment demand. For most of the review period, CNH traded at a premium to CNY, averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained stable. Although overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations because of occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, it remained below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). Three-month CNH HIBOR declined in tandem with onshore renminbi interest rates in late December, before rising again in late January, partly because of tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixing In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand. Since the fourth quarter, growth in renminbi deposits accelerated, reflecting to some extent the appreciation of the renminbi and its higher interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with end-June 2020, growth in the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit accelerated, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of this total, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit declined by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi businesses, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% over the seven months since end-June 2020 to RMB159.2 billion. Meanwhile, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by local banks amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, representing year-on-year growth of 16.7%. Among these transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland increased faster than remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a sizeable renminbi liquidity pool, sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. In 2020, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system was as high as RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

As the economic downturn persisted amid recurring waves of the COVID-19 pandemic, compounded by the prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound, underpinned by its strong capital and liquidity position. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activity can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and persistent geopolitical tensions will adversely affect business activity and continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the related downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, from 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that outweighed the modest increase in non-interest income and thereby reducing profit. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, while the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely driven by substantial fund inflows arising from equity market activity, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate, a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, followed a broadly similar trend, falling markedly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks Looking ahead, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to adversely affect banks’ net interest margins, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. In addition, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of the economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the banking sector’s loan quality and profitability in the near term. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated AIs stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirements also indicated a stable funding position among AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for AIs, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all AIs, broadly similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs As the total deposits of all AIs increased in the second half of 2020 while total lending declined over the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, at the end of 2020, from 86.4% and 65.5%, respectively, six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained relatively low in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock involving a 200-basis-point rise in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a persistent economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tightened social-distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, total credit in the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although the pace of growth slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, the total loans and advances of all AIs declined by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total lending was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans, including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance, and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, during the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, after declining by 2.0% in the first half of the year, Hong Kong dollar loans at the end of 2020 remained broadly at the same level as at the end of June. Following substantial growth of 10.6% in the first half of 2020, foreign currency loans declined by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting lower demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector became slightly more optimistic about the near-term credit demand outlook than it had been six months earlier. The HKMA’s December 2020 Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook showed that the proportion of respondent AIs expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decline over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment capability of households and corporates, banks’ loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio of all AIs rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy remained weak, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify across the world, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks and the possibility that monetary tightening may be more aggressive than expected if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. If the US Fed tightens monetary policy substantially, leading to tighter global financial conditions, the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies will come under pressure. The recent outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have significant repercussions for the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, growth in total bank lending accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the ongoing economic recovery, while the potentially faster-than-expected normalisation of US monetary policy will also pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness continuing into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on mobility worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and spread across a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. More recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices may further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties. In the near term, large-scale pandemic outbreaks could lead to the reimposition of lockdowns and a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks. In the United States, as the risk of inflation proving more persistent and broad-based than expected has increased, the US Fed has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating its timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. If the US Fed needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions may also tighten, weakening borrowers’ debt servicing ability, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. The recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, aggravate shortages in the supply of industrial products, and heighten financial market volatility. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressure on OEFs, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for OEFs, can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the recovery momentum temporarily slowed when some Southeast Asian economies reimposed stringent anti-pandemic measures in the third quarter, while the region’s technology-exporting economies, namely South Korea and Singapore, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for regional economies with lower vaccination rates and strained public health resources. Second, the US Fed’s accelerated policy normalisation may trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressure. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support the economic recovery will face an increasingly difficult trade-off between containing capital outflow pressure and supporting economic activity. Third, the slowdown in major economies, together with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the trade growth outlook. Fourth, increases in the prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Coupled with increased uncertainty in the global economy, this will further complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. Over the longer term, to rebuild a sustainable and resilient growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is affected by corporates’ environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing and measures to tighten the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term owing to the continued property market downturn and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. The Mainland authorities have therefore made stabilising growth their top priority this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Both the total amount of onshore bond defaults and defaults on onshore bonds issued by state-owned enterprises declined in the second half of 2021. Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks, particularly systemically important banks, have limited exposure to loans to property developers, as well as low NPL ratios and high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately, as merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the ongoing global economic recovery, improving local labour market conditions and the Government’s launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, its first full year of positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social-distancing measures put pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022–23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flows, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and the various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced by raising maximum loan amounts and extending application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme until the end of October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, although growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from the expansion of the global economy. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The Government projects real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth estimate of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to the uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end. Total employment rallied but remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures had re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also pointed to fewer new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tighter anti-pandemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in industries involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months, partly owing to price increases for meals away from home and certain energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term amid higher import prices and pandemic-related disruptions to logistics. However, weak rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast is for a headline inflation rate of 2.4% in 2022, while the Government projects a headline inflation rate of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar briefly rallied slightly in October 2021, its appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly owing to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the US Fed normalised monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range for most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Trading in Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. With ample interbank liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained low during the review period. The average new-mortgage lending rate edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to flourish. In particular, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit rising to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022. Although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased to RMB1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from its efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way, northbound and southbound Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect; the continued opening of the Mainland capital account; increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets; and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets generally higher in the final quarter of 2021, taking the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices and escalating Russia-Ukraine tensions have led major global equity markets to consolidate since early January 2022.

Owing to the rapid global spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressure continued to intensify and spread across a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the Fed’s monetary policy stance, increasing the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could put currently elevated asset valuations under pressure and adversely affect emerging markets where the recovery generally continued to lag. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine drove up energy and other commodity prices and triggered global financial market volatility, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant in the region, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with the region’s major exporters of technology products continuing to outperform other economies. Although the Omicron variant is unlikely to seriously impede the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cloud the economic outlook for the region. In addition, the normalisation of Fed policy could trigger a correction in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies could weigh on growth in goods exports in the region. On the one hand, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up commodity prices and increased inflation risk; on the other hand, it could weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, complicating regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of coronavirus infections, power restrictions and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from the cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the government has made stabilising growth its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policies will also provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the spread of the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with that of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter mobility restrictions worldwide. In addition, supply chain problems, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to put production under pressure. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China, which offset the expected growth rally in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF projections of real GDP growth Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressure continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose markedly in major advanced economies, particularly the United States, which had implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic began. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressure spread across a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine drove up the prices of various commodities and may exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressure. Chart 2.2 Core CPI inflation rates in selected economies (1) The latest data for the United States, the United Kingdom and the Euro area are for January 2022, while those for the other economies are for December 2021. (2) “Advanced Asian economies” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) “Emerging Asian economies” include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainty, with downside risks predominating, and will depend on the development of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment evolves, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far responded to the recent surge in Omicron cases with targeted measures focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less stringent measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown preliminary signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, in the event of a large-scale outbreak, lockdown measures may be reintroduced, leading to a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index—supplier delivery times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief from goods inflation. However, several developments could cause the current high level of global inflation to persist longer than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imported from Russia will push up commodity prices; the lagged pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices; the possibility that the earlier sharp rise in global residential property prices will drive up future rentals; the upside risk posed by tight labour markets to wage growth; and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Fed shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 meeting of the Federal Open Markets Committee, no longer characterising high inflation as “transitory”, doubling the pace of asset-purchase tapering from US$15 billion to US$30 billion per month with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing suggested that the Fed might raise interest rates several times during 2022. In contrast, given the Euro area’s closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the ECB may face more difficult policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, coupled with persistently elevated global debt levels and asset valuations after a prolonged period of policy easing, if persistent inflationary pressure requires the US Fed to tighten policy more rapidly than expected, borrowers’ debt servicing ability may be at risk of deterioration and financial market volatility could be triggered. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe intensified, risk aversion in financial markets increased and signs of US dollar shortages emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Amid a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressure on OEFs, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for OEFs, can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as major exporters of technology products in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the unevenness of the recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressure remained moderate in several emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index The market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, but the near-term economic outlook for the region faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread throughout the region since the end of 2021, its economic impact has remained milder than that of previous waves of infection. However, some regional economies with lagging vaccination rates and relatively constrained public health resources will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, Fed policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support the economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between containing capital outflow pressure and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in long-term US yields could also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, increasing the risk of corrections in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between ten-year Asian sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the outlook for merchandise trade in the region faces uncertainty from the slowdown in major economies and a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which could weaken export growth in the region. Chart 2.6 United States: imports from emerging Asia and real GDP Fourth, although regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, conflict-induced increases in commodity prices will feed through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, this will complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted regional economies to the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to attach greater importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporates’ environmental performance. The coronavirus pandemic dealt a severe blow to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some OEFs experienced substantial fund outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Fund outflows from selected OEFs during the March 2020 episode Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another possible reason for the substantial fund outflows was that investors exercised a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming their fund holdings early, thereby avoiding redemption costs that could rise sharply during periods of market stress. To curb outflows arising from the first-mover advantage, some OEFs use swing pricing—an OEF pricing rule that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many OEFs used swing pricing during this episode, no empirical study had established whether swing pricing could effectively reduce outflows from OEFs. Against this backdrop, this box conducts an empirical study to determine whether swing pricing reduced fund outflows from OEFs during the March 2020 episode and thereby lowered their liquidity risk. In addition, this box seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors and thereby shifting redemption costs to them. The first-mover advantage mainly exists in OEFs that use traditional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs incurred by fund investors, such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments, are reflected in OEF prices only after the transactions have taken place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear these transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, particularly when substantial redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced because redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by OEFs.

With merchandise exports and private consumption continuing to grow, the Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, returning to positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of the local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity. The overall economy is expected to maintain its recovery for 2022 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the recovery will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the epidemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the labour market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the short term amid higher import prices, weak local rentals and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth slowed compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first year of positive full-year growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). On the domestic front, improved labour market conditions, together with the Government’s implementation of the Consumption Voucher Scheme, boosted private consumption. However, aggregate investment spending declined in the final quarter after two consecutive quarters of strong rallies. On the external front, amid the ongoing global economic recovery, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance remained robust, while trade in services stayed weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Chart 3.2). On a net basis, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volumes A new wave of the local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022–23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and their application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is likewise applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the ongoing epidemic and a higher base effect. In particular, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s advancement of various public works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The Government projects real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the growth estimates of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalisation and heightened geopolitical concerns, such as the Russia–Ukraine situation, have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could stimulate local economic growth. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rallied by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, although it remained below the pre-epidemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures had re-emerged amid a new wave of the local epidemic. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also pointed to fewer new vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of the local epidemic and tightened anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the short term, particularly on sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on local epidemic developments and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, as local demand recovered and external prices rose (Chart 3.5), prices for meals out and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the CCPI continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained weak, they rose slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong import prices Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.7 Unit labour costs Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term amid higher import prices and epidemic-induced disruptions to logistics. However, weak rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast is for headline inflation to reach 2.4% in 2022, while the Government projects headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022.

Amid risk aversion in the local stock market and concerns over US monetary policy normalization, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. With ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained low. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar exchange and money market continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding shocks arising from volatility in fund flows. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rallied slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly because of weak southbound net buying through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Fed’s monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, initial public offering fundraising activity continued to support the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of unusual cross-border capital flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Southbound net buying through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable owing to the appreciation of the RMB against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the very small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As US interest rates rise, outflows of Hong Kong dollar funding—the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions—may, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), cause the Hong Kong dollar to weaken and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding volatility in fund flows without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuance of bills to meet banks’ continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion during the review period to HK$1,188.7 billion, with the Aggregate Balance before Discount Window activities correspondingly decreasing by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. It should, however, be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate because of various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities, and it is therefore appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Overall, trading in Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Given ample liquidity in the banking system, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained low despite market concerns over US monetary tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of increased funding demand toward year-end, HIBOR edged up in December 2021. The average new-mortgage lending rate rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, the ample liquidity in the banking system can provide a sufficient buffer during large-scale capital market activities or periods of financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates During the review period, the CNH interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand toward year-end, overnight CNH HIBOR fluctuated slightly in late December 2021, while three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixing In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3% to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Of this amount, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong During the six-month period from July 2021, although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), representing an increase of 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period a year earlier. Hong Kong’s large renminbi liquidity pool continued to support substantial volumes of renminbi payments and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi RTGS system increased from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Flow of renminbi trade settlement payments Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deeper regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Major global equity markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but underwent a correction from January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong equity market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by sharp declines in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainty over pandemic developments in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a nearly two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, the CNH debt market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market had softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weaker asset market sentiment and a new local wave of the pandemic. Major global equity markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, driving the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). Stimulus from government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings supported the rise in major global equity markets, although the pandemic remained investors’ principal risk concern throughout the year. However, major global equity markets underwent a correction from early January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies in response to sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. By contrast, Hong Kong’s equity market continued to lag behind other major global equity markets at the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November and closed at 23,398 at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, renewed buying interest from value investors in Hong Kong’s equity market pushed the Hang Seng Index back up to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainty over pandemic developments in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points at the end of February. Over the entire review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index declined by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index With the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, equity-market option-implied volatility fluctuated sharply in late November 2021 before subsiding. Although the SKEW Index retreated from its record high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors’ concerns that the equity market’s prolonged rally since the outbreak of the pandemic would undergo a correction and their willingness to commit more capital to hedge against downside equity-market risks (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatility of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and the SKEW Index Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong equity market continued to record net inflows from international investors since the previous report (Chart 4.13). By contrast, Southbound Stock Connect recorded substantial net fund outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly because of concerns over the impact of changes in Mainland regulation on technology stocks. However, buying flows through Southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording total inflows of HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, cumulative net buying increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net fund inflows into Hong Kong’s equity market Chart 4.14 Net flows through equity-market connectivity schemes After raising a record amount of funds in the first half of 2021, Hong Kong’s primary market slowed in the second half. For 2021 as a whole, there were 98 initial public offerings, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), with total funds raised declining by 17.8% from the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global initial public offering market, behind only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Hong Kong initial public offering market The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. Monetary policy easing in the Mainland and more secondary listings in Hong Kong by US-listed Chinese companies in the primary market will improve sentiment in Hong Kong’s equity market. However, the equity market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainty over pandemic developments in Hong Kong, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalization, and escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Profitability of Hong Kong retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by robust capitalisation and liquidity, the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound. During the review period, the HKMA extended a number of support measures to further assist the economy through difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, while the risk that US monetary policy normalization may proceed faster than expected will also present challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was mainly attributable to declines in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, from 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Reflecting the continued impact of the low-interest-rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks also remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA’s increased issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, HIBOR recorded a slight increase in the final quarter of 2021. However, as liquidity in the banking system remained highly abundant, HIBOR continued to stay at a relatively low level. Specifically, three-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The funding cost of retail banks remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding cost, rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Since June 2019, the composite interest rate has been calculated in accordance with the newly implemented local interest rate risk in the banking book framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those for previous months. From a broader perspective, the aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong rose slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks Since June 2019, all licensed banks required to comply with the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The aggregate funding cost has been calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those for previous months. Although the normalization of US monetary policy may signal an improvement in bank profitability, the near-term improvement may be partly offset by two factors. First, despite the US Fed’s indication that there would be multiple rate hikes in 2022, past experience suggests that movements in local interest rates may lag behind those in US interest rates, especially when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains highly abundant. It may therefore take more time for improvements in banks’ net interest margins to materialize. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may create uncertainty over the pace of economic recovery, thereby exerting pressure on banks’ asset quality and profitability. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated AIs was 20.2% at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.5), well above the international minimum requirement of 8%. The Tier 1 capital ratio and Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2%, respectively, during the period. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs stood at a robust level of 7.9% at the end of 2021, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3%. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Since 1 January 2013, locally incorporated AIs have been required to comply with the revised Basel III capital adequacy framework. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions remained high at 151.9% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.6), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 59.1%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1.
