Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted considerable efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 as a standalone report for the first time this year. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of the banking system in Hong Kong to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and putting into practice our role as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA’s key functions. The report sets out our specific initiatives and work, with the following key highlights: Banks are exposed to climate risk in their day-to-day operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks’ resilience to climate change. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and explored how technology could be used to help banks assess the impacts of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we also shared with the industry good practices for the proper management of these products, with a view to enhancing banks’ climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in collaborative initiatives to address climate risk and promote the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework, which will increase transparency in the financial market and promote greater alignment among green finance policies. Internationally, we actively participate in a number of international organisations, helping to formulate policies for addressing climate change and assess its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable finance. Although 2022 was a particularly challenging year for the global bond market, the volume of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth, increasing by 42% to a total of US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the Hainan Provincial People’s Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The vigorous growth of Hong Kong’s green bond market is also partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two “firsts”. In May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural government green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion, which were then the world’s largest green retail bond issuance. We also assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural tokenised green bond in February 2023. This was the world’s first tokenised green bond issued by a government, and the issuance was also a milestone marking our successful integration of Hong Kong’s strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data and talent are indispensable to the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment requires efforts and collaboration across different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to developing the local green classification framework described above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training for the industry and enhances Hong Kong’s data resources through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance. The Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas, including mandatory climate-related disclosures and opportunities in the carbon market. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, notably by setting a target of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and long-term risk-adjusted returns. In addition, to fully capture the potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment by the Exchange Fund and identifying investment opportunities that support the climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the portfolio’s long-term returns. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had fallen by 43% from its 2017 level. In fact, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to carbon-intensive assets has consistently remained lower than that of the overall market. Going forward, we will continue progressing towards our net-zero emissions target by further integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, exercising active ownership, maintaining collaboration with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: the environment, our people and social responsibility. On the environment, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and more environmentally friendly markets for the wider community; on our people, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment; and on social responsibility, we are committed to enhancing financial literacy among the public, promoting financial inclusion and actively giving back to the community. Compared with the levels recorded when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption all achieved double-digit reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the near term, our target is to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 from the 2015 baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration among multiple parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must take concrete action, lead by example, and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s near-term plans and priorities for addressing climate change across its key functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in reaching this goal. We are confident that, through the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the wider community, we can successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong’s financial sector and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development of and best practices in green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking sector, we will work to strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing regulatory requirements for climate risk management, incorporate climate considerations into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector’s “Greenness Baseline.” The HKMA will also support banks’ efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing as part of the regular regulator-led stress-testing exercise for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to address climate risk under an enhanced stress-testing framework covering a range of stress scenarios, including extreme climate events and adverse economic conditions. To promote the sound development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector’s green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in increasing the issuance of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and expanding the Programme’s scope to cover sustainability bonds, while attracting more green finance activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions, and corporate entities to undertake green finance activities through Hong Kong and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. Separately, through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, we will continue to collaborate with other agencies and departments on cross-sectoral issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will jointly launch various dedicated programmes in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market insights, offering targeted professional training to banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop road maps for making green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme and expand its influence across Asia. The Alliance will also further enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead project initiatives in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, demonstrating its commitment to participating in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social, and governance factors into its investment management processes, strive towards its net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares about its employees as well as the wider community and surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability road map and established climate targets for our own operations, demonstrating our commitment to global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise reducing carbon emissions and encourage employees to provide their full support by conserving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide employees with further guidance on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To advance digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications, further improve work efficiency, and minimise as far as possible any potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are affected by various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital into green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the regulator of the banking sector, the HKMA has placed particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risk, while accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas including environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how the existing Basel Framework addresses such risks. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue working to incorporate climate-related factors into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1, “Climate Risk Management,” in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges relating to the implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into its banking supervisory processes and communicated the plan to the banking sector in June. As part of implementing the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1, “Risk-based Supervisory Approach,” and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, drawing on experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined its climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA also developed a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular regulator-led stress-testing exercise, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its greenness assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. During the thematic reviews, the HKMA identified a number of sound practices and shared them with the industry through a circular issued in December, enabling banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks’ capacity to manage climate risk. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions could facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices; its work in this area employs advanced analytics and compliance technology, complemented by fully automated collection of supervisory data. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the collection of anti-money laundering supervisory data to reduce banks’ manual workload and paper consumption. To enhance transparency across financial markets and improve the consistency of green finance policies, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. Commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, the framework classifies economic activities as green or sustainable and provides a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore the framework’s features and challenges in depth, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the framework’s structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognising that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analyses and research to strengthen its ongoing surveillance. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of risks to financial stability and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream of the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022 to examine two major topics in depth: greenwashing in the corporate green bond market3 and the role of disclosures in mitigating exposure to climate risk4. The findings of these studies help inform the formulation of policy and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Locally, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a broad range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and the HKMA’s Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s “Liquidity Facilities Framework” is a collateralised standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps promote international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, while drawing lessons from these discussions to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA stepped up efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and drivers, support international initiatives, and align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government’s climate strategies1. The Steering Group’s work is primarily guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out six key areas of focus and five action points to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future together (Figure 1). Enhance climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre; promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhance practitioners’ relevant skills and strengthen public awareness and understanding; encourage product innovation and research initiatives to direct capital flows towards green and sustainable projects; seize opportunities arising from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into the green finance centre of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area); and strengthen regional and international collaboration. Actions to date in advancing the development of sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Its current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), a green taxonomy (see “Developing a Green Classification Framework to Facilitate Green Finance” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. In particular, the Steering Group announced in March its preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong and will support Hong Kong’s development as a regional carbon trading centre, including by developing a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalising on opportunities arising from collaboration in the Greater Bay Area. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of the collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting unlisted firms and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which facilitates corporate sustainability reporting while helping financial institutions collect and analyse corporate-level data for risk assessments and related business decisions. This represents an important step in expanding the coverage of the Steering Group’s data work to include SMEs, an important segment of the economy that has traditionally been difficult to reach. In July 2021, the Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance to coordinate the efforts of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions in training and policy development, and to establish resource and data repositories. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories covering data, training information and internship opportunities, respectively, helping the financial sector and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To support the training of industry talent, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other initiatives to promote skills training included launching the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module3 under the HKMA’s Enhanced Competency Framework for banking practitioners. Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks4, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions and innovation and technology providers to jointly develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to realise their full potential in making green finance a mainstream core business and to promote the financial system’s participation in global climate change-related activities. Operating model: provide financial institutions with a one-stop peer-learning platform through which they can acquire the knowledge, tools and information needed to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; bring together green finance leaders, connect green financial institutions across different emerging markets, facilitate communication, and explore frontier topics; advance the global green finance agenda and unlock limitless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became cornerstone members of the Alliance and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities, thereby facilitating the transition to a green economy. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpages (English version): Cornerstone Members; International Finance Corporation and HKMA Sign Memorandum of Understanding. Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has held a total of 18 training events and roundtable meetings, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022, the Alliance and the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7 published their first frontier research report, entitled “Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulatory Oversight.” The HKMA has continued to promote green and sustainable debt issuance and foster a local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022, including bonds and loans, reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promote green finance, and develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in implementing the related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued nearly US$16 billion equivalent in institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the Programme’s transparency and accountability arrangements, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable members of the public to participate in and share the benefits of Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment, the inaugural batch of retail green bonds, totalling HK$20 billion, was issued in May and received an enthusiastic response from the public, making it the world’s largest retail green bond issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable financial products in Hong Kong, consolidating Hong Kong’s position as a leading green finance hub regionally and internationally. The Government also continued its regular institutional green bond issuances in the 2022–23 financial year and issued US$5.75 billion equivalent in green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency offering covered US dollars, euros and RMB, with tenors ranging from two to 30 years, continuing to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The offering was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government’s previous green bond issuances, reflecting investor confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit profile and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the RMB bonds to RMB10 billion. The shares allocated to international investors and Mainland investors participating through Southbound Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong’s position as a leading CNH business hub and further consolidating its leadership as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology in bond issuance and settlement. It was among the world’s first government-issued tokenised green bonds. The primary issuance was settled on a private blockchain network on a T+1 basis, while subsequent processes, including coupon payments, secondary-market trade settlement and redemption at maturity, were also digitalised. The experience gained from this Government issuance may serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region, respectively. The International Capital Market Association’s report showed that Hong Kong became Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances in 2022, with bonds arranged in Hong Kong totalling US$27.8 billion, accounting for more than approximately one-third of the regional total. Asia’s largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances: US$27.8 billion. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB5 billion of offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion in green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also issued RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlighted Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its long-standing position as the region’s leading fundraising platform. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in 2021, using the Scheme to attract more related professional service providers, including financial institutions, green consultants and external review bodies, to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been well received by the industry. By the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the costs of pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both types of external review services for issuers of more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum used credit line threshold for external review cost subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller corporates obtain green finance. Following the successful completion of a proof of concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digital carbon forwards, also known as mitigation outcome interests (MOIs), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022 and successfully developed two prototypes using blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digital MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in support of the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, required its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrated environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth next,” the HKMA believes that giving due regard to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance its responsible investment journey, including by setting a “net-zero emissions by 2050” target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategies to strengthen portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better long-term risk-adjusted returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, working with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment and collaborating with international organisations to formulate ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a crucial role in managing climate risk. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures concerning the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Financial Stability Board’s Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). a. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to give priority to ESG investments with long-term risk-adjusted returns comparable to those of other projects, in line with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investment projects. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors progress in integrating ESG factors into investments and the Exchange Fund’s ESG profile through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s various ESG initiatives. The proposals discussed and progress of work at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Oversight and Governance Structure for Responsible Investment The dedicated team in the Risk Management and Compliance Division works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on integrating ESG factors and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investment projects: Public Market Investments The Credit, Rules and Compliance Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Compliance Division participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Striving to Exercise Active Ownership” in the “Risk Management” section on page 27 for details). Private Market Investments The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal conducted by the Risk Management and Compliance Division and the private market investment teams. Concrete evidence² continues to demonstrate the significant impacts of climate change and related risks. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming that the announced “nationally determined contribution” targets of all jurisdictions are fully implemented, the increase in global temperature by 2100 is still estimated to be as high as 2.1°C to 2.4°C, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting the increase in global average temperature to below 2°C above pre-industrial levels. If jurisdictions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and market repricing of assets based on anticipated future trends, together with inherent physical risks, will intensify pressure on asset valuations. In view of updates to global warming trajectories and panel data model assumptions, the HKMA drew on the expertise of external consultants to further assess, in addition to the scenarios evaluated in 2021, the resilience of the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” under the “Rapid Transition” scenario (Figure 2). The “Rapid Transition” scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while various assets are abruptly divested to keep the increase in average temperature within 1.5°C by 2100. This scenario is broadly consistent with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The “Investment Portfolio” remains resilient over the medium to long term because a relatively large proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds that are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sector distribution is critical. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets may benefit from the transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may adversely affect performance in the short term, particularly that of equity assets. The “Investment Portfolio” as a whole will be increasingly affected by physical risks that gradually emerge over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Like other panel data model methodologies, climate scenarios have their limitations. The analysis is based on the sector distribution of market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level and does not take into account the effects of actively selecting specific securities within a sector. More in-depth research indicates that the investments in the “Investment Portfolio” are generally more resilient to transition shocks or less adversely affected than the strategic asset allocation market benchmarks. This result further confirms that the HKMA’s responsible investment approach, with its focus on combating climate change, can enhance portfolio resilience. The climate change trajectory remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities arising from climate change. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investment and seizing opportunities relating to climate transition, climate risk mitigation and enhanced long-term portfolio returns. The HKMA maintained its strong momentum in 2022, further increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainability bonds by 50%. In terms of equity investment, the HKMA invested in an actively managed governance-themed equity portfolio and adopted a decarbonisation strategy for passive equity portfolios that tilts towards companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with the dedicated general partners of the Exchange Fund’s “Long-Term Growth Portfolio” the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Figure 3). Figure 3 Ongoing Measures to Increase ESG Investments The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator that, in addition to generating clean energy, places strong emphasis on social factors and biodiversity. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from attacking their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vulture species. Livestock are important assets for local villagers. To help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to safeguard the animals against natural predators. In addition, the operator employs a bird-monitoring team to issue alerts when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left behind by predators, allowing the wind turbines to be shut down to prevent vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win outcome: it safeguards the villagers’ livelihoods while reducing fatal collisions between vultures and wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can create additional business opportunities and open up revenue streams for corporate entities, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operations. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China specialising in logistics services for cold-chain pharmaceuticals, chemical products and high-end consumer goods. The company faces increasingly stringent ESG operating standards, primarily because multinational corporate customers require their service providers to meet ambitious decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these requirements, the company engaged an external consultant to help formulate a “Three-Year ESG Plan” aimed at reducing carbon-emission intensity by 50% by 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan delivered significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures earned the company recognition from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing as a “Low-Carbon Green Management Case.” These achievements and recognition enabled the company to secure substantial business opportunities, particularly from multinational corporate customers in the consumer goods and chemical products sectors that place strong emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its fourth annual ESG Workshop, where it exchanged sound ESG practices with nine participating private market institutions, including general partners, limited partners and corporate entities, and promoted sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public markets, the HKMA encouraged trading partners, mainly investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr Howard Lee, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivers the opening remarks at the HKMA ESG Workshop 2022 At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in formulating industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a PRI-coordinated joint initiative among signatories to develop a standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaire⁵, ⁶ for private equity and venture capital investments, helping private market investors conduct ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in several working groups supporting FCLTGlobal’s research, which examines leading market practices for long-term portfolios and the decarbonisation of private assets, as well as the application of those practices by long-term investors. As an NGFS member and TCFD supporter, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS Guide on Climate-related Disclosure for Central Banks, demonstrating its commitment to adopting sound ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a subgroup under the NGFS “Net Zero for Central Banks” workstream and participates in developing sustainable and responsible investment approaches for the central bank community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars to share insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies.
